summary: To tackle the challenge of fragmented satellite fire records, we developed the Harmonized Burning Activity Calendar- a high-performance, full-stack climate platform that unifies 24 years of NASA Earth observation data into a continuous, interactive fire activity timeline alongside live near-real-time hotspot surveillance. Long-term wildfire monitoring is severely hindered by an observational discontinuity: merging NASA’s legacy 1 km MODIS sensor with the newer 375 m VIIRS sensor creates false fire escalation alarms due to differing spatial resolutions and sensitivities. Our platform directly solves this challenge by implementing an automated Medallion data engineering pipeline that calibrates Fire Radiative Power (FRP) and harmonizes sensor overlaps, establishing a statistically consistent baseline queried via DuckDB in milliseconds. This work is critical because MODIS is approaching decommissioning; without intelligent cross-sensor harmonization, climate scientists, disaster response teams, and environmental policymakers risk losing historical decadal context. By bridging satellite generations into a single seamless record, our tool prevents analytical distortions, detects true climate anomalies, and empowers emergency responders to mitigate wildfire crises with validated, continuous data.
details:
To overcome the severe observational discontinuity between NASA’s legacy 1 km MODIS and modern 375 m VIIRS instruments, we engineered the Harmonized Burning Activity Calendar around a multi-tiered data science and calibration pipeline. Rather than applying a naive statistical scale factor, our approach exploits the 12-year operational overlap between Terra/Aqua and S-NPP/NOAA-20 to establish cross-sensor consistency. In our Medallion data engineering architecture, the Silver Tier ingests raw spatiotemporal point clouds and performs spatiotemporal co-location to isolate simultaneous observations. We then apply dual-metric harmonization: first, calibrating Fire Radiative Power (FRP)-a physical proxy for combustion rate that remains far more stable across sensor foot-prints than raw hotspot counts; and second, computing dynamic grid-level scaling ratios that account for VIIRS’s enhanced sensitivity to sub-pixel, low-intensity burns without distorting high-intensity crown fires. This yields a harmonized baseline where a 2003 MODIS fire detection and a 2024 VIIRS observation can finally be compared on an ecologically true, apples-to-apples scale.

We operationalized this methodology into a high-performance web platform built on a Python FastAPI backend and an embedded DuckDB columnar engine querying compressed Apache Parquet tables. By avoiding heavy, traditional spatial databases, the application executes complex polygon clipping and 24-year aggregation queries over millions of data points in under 50 milliseconds directly in the browser. Users interact through a React and Leaflet GIS interface centered on our "Wall of Fire"—a 365-day by 24-year matrix heatmap that maps calibrated fire intensity against historical day-of-year baselines, accompanied by cumulative seasonal burn curves and live NASA FIRMS API streaming. When designing the system, our team carefully balanced astronomical orbital geometries, sensor swath-edge distortions, and real-world field constraints, incorporating graceful API fallbacks for low-bandwidth forestry stations. By transforming raw, conflicting satellite feeds into a mathematically coherent and visually intuitive timeline, our platform empowers forest managers, climate researchers, and disaster response teams to detect genuine multi-decadal anomalies and act before critical tipping points are breached.
